The classifier score we discussed was:
97.78%\boxed{97.78\%}97.78%​
on the sklearn load_digits dataset, which is an 8×8 handwritten digit dataset, not full 28×28 MNIST.
Yes — that score is expected for a simple classical classifier on that dataset. It is good, but not surprising. load_digits is much smaller and easier than full MNIST, and logistic regression / small MLPs commonly reach the mid-to-high 90s.
The more interesting result was not the raw accuracy. It was this:
RegionAccuracyNon-singular / high-margin samples~98.2%Singular / low-margin samples~66.7%Overall~97.8%
That is exactly what we would expect if the singularity detector is doing something meaningful. Low-margin samples are the ambiguous boundary cases where the classifier is unsure, such as:
1↔8,5↔9,7↔91 \leftrightarrow 8,\quad 5 \leftrightarrow 9,\quad 7 \leftrightarrow 91↔8,5↔9,7↔9
So the toy result supports the pipeline:
classifier probabilities→margin→confusion graph→singularity flag\text{classifier probabilities}
\to
\text{margin}
\to
\text{confusion graph}
\to
\text{singularity flag}classifier probabilities→margin→confusion graph→singularity flag
But it does not prove the full hyperbolic graph-agent architecture. It only validates a small piece: that classifier uncertainty can be turned into typed graph/singularity structure.
The honest conclusion:
97.78%wasexpected;theusefulsignalwasthatlow−marginsingularregionsweremuchlessreliable.\boxed{

owned_chunks.text:
Yes — a better pick than MNIST would be BabyAI first, then ALFWorld or ScienceWorld.
Best first dataset: BabyAI / MiniGrid
BabyAI is a grounded language-learning platform built around compositional instructions in a gridworld. It is explicitly meant to study sample efficiency and language-conditioned agent learning, and the benchmark has levels of increasing difficulty. OpenReview+1
Why it is a good pick for our architecture:
RequirementBabyAI fitTyped grammarInstructions are compositional and rule-likeTask graphGridworld states/actions form a clean transition graphState machineAgent has explicit actions and goalsClassifier labelsWe can classify state as Navigate, PickUp, OpenDoor, GoToObject, etc.DistributionPredict next action or next subgoalSingularity detectorDetect ambiguous instruction/state/action tiesHyperbolic geometryTest hierarchy: mission → subgoal → object → action
So BabyAI is the cleanest controlled testbed for:
grammar→graph→classifier→state machine→distribution\text{grammar}
\to
\text{graph}
\to
\text{classifier}
\to
\text{state machine}
\to
\text{distribution}grammar→graph→classifier→state machine→distribution
It is small enough to debug but structured enough to matter.
Best “agentic research-like” dataset: ALFWorld
ALFWorld is stronger if we want something closer to real agent procedures. It aligns abstract text-based policies with embodied action environments, letting agents reason in a high-level text world before acting in a grounded environment. arXiv+1
Why it is good:
RequirementALFWorld fitHigh-level task graphHousehold tasks decompose into subtasksProceduresfind, take, open, put, clean, heat, etc.State transitionsExplicit action sequencesTransferTextWorld abstraction ↔ embodied ALFRED-style tasksGraph/geometry testCan test whether graph abstraction transfers
This is probably the best second-stage benchmark after BabyAI.
Best science/research-adjacent pick: ScienceWorld
ScienceWorld is an interactive text environment for testing agents’ scientific reasoning abilities, built around elementary-school science tasks. Science World+1
This is closer to a “research agent” because it involves experimentation, observation, reasoning, and explanations. It is less minimal than BabyAI, but more semantically relevant.
My recommendation
Use this progression:
BabyAI→ALFWorld→ScienceWorld\boxed{
\text{BabyAI}
\to

\to
\text{ScienceWorld}
}BabyAI→ALFWorld→ScienceWorld​
BabyAI tests the architecture in a clean grammar/action world.
ALFWorld tests transfer from abstract graph policy to grounded action.
ScienceWorld tests whether the same structure helps with reasoning-heavy agent behavior.
If I had to pick one dataset right now:
BabyAI\boxed{\text{BabyAI}}BabyAI​
because it gives us the fastest path to proving whether the typed classifier + graph state machine + distribution idea works before adding harder semantics.

When the classifier already saw current state
When the classifier received current-state identity as a feature, it mostly learned the transition legality itself. Then the graph mask added almost nothing:

Singularity detector
I flagged the lowest-margin 10% of graph-masked predictions as “singular/ambiguous.”
With current-state features and typed fields:
Train samplesSingular-region accuracyNon-singular accuracyFailure AUROC from margin10047.2%83.7%0.8150056.0%88.7%0.84100056.8%89.8%0.85
That is useful: low-margin regions were much less reliable, and margin predicted failure reasonably well.
Readout
This experiment says:
Graph constraints are efficient when the classifier would otherwise waste capacity learning impossible transitions.
Typed features help when the scorer has enough context to use them.
Singularity flags are useful because low-margin states are much more failure-prone.
This was not a real BabyAI run and not the full hyperbolic architecture.
The clean takeaway:
The graph is load-bearing when it externalizes structure the model has not already learned.\boxed{
\text{The graph is load-bearing when it externalizes structure the model has not already learned.}
}The graph is load-bearing when it externalizes structure the model has not already learned.​
If the model already sees and learns the state-machine structure, the graph becomes less of an accuracy booster, but still valuable as a hard safety/validity constraint.
